Start a simple first page in a notebook

A **business record** is anything written down that shows what happened in your business: a sale, a purchase, money you paid out, goods you gave on credit, money that came in by transfer. It can be a line in a notebook, a receipt, a POS slip, or an entry in a phone app. The important thing is that it is **written at the time it happens**, so you do not need to remember it later.

Writing it down at the moment it happens is the whole secret of record-keeping.

Many market traders keep everything in their head. That works when you sell one product to a few people. It stops working when you have ten products, five customers buying on credit, two suppliers, school fees to pay and a POS agent sending transfers. The head forgets, mixes things up, and remembers the good days more than the bad ones. Paper and phones do not forget.
Who uses your records?

**You**, to know if you are really making money and which goods sell best.
**Your family or a helper**, so the shop can run when you are sick or travelling.
**Your cooperative, esusu group or microfinance bank**, when you ask for a loan.
**A business partner or supplier**, who wants to see that you pay and sell steadily.
**A grant or training programme**, which often asks how much you sell in a month.
Money in your hand is not the same as profit

This is the most important idea in the whole course. At the end of a busy day you may have a lot of cash in your bag. But part of that money must go back to buy new stock. Part of it pays for transport, market levy and the boy who helps you carry loads. Only what is left after all those costs is **profit**. Without records you cannot see the difference, and many traders end up spending their capital (the money that runs the business) thinking it is profit.

Worked example: Bisi's pepper stall, one day
For example, Bisi sells fresh pepper and tomatoes in a Lagos market. She buys from a supplier in the morning and sells all day. Amounts are approximate.
She buys a basket of tomatoes for about ₦18,000 and a bag of pepper for about ₦12,000. Total stock bought: ₦30,000.
She pays transport of about ₦2,000 and market ticket of about ₦500.
By evening she counts ₦38,000 in her bag.
Without a record she thinks: "I made ₦38,000 today."
With a record she calculates: ₦38,000 minus ₦30,000 stock minus ₦2,500 costs = ₦5,500.
Bisi's real profit for the day is about ₦5,500, not ₦38,000. If she spends ₦10,000 on household things tonight, she has eaten into the money she needs to buy tomorrow's stock.

You do not need to buy anything special. A 40 or 60 leaf exercise book, a biro and a ruler are enough to begin. Draw lines with the ruler so each page has columns.
What makes a good record
**Dated**: every page and every line has the date.
**Complete**: every sale and every cost, even small ones like ₦200 sachet water for customers.
**Honest**: write what really happened, not what you wish happened.
**Kept safe**: away from rain, children and rats, in a nylon bag or a box.
**Easy to read**: one line for one thing, numbers written clearly.

If you cannot read or write well, you can still keep records. Use pictures or symbols for each product (a drawing of a tomato, a bottle, a bag of rice), use tally marks for each item sold, and ask a trusted child or friend to write the totals at night. Some traders send a WhatsApp voice note to themselves after each sale and write it down in the evening. The method matters less than doing it every day.

A simple first page needs only a few things: the **date** at the top, a column for **what happened** ("sold 3 tins of tomato paste" or "paid keke"), a column for **money in** and a column for **money out**. At the bottom of the day, draw a line and write the two totals. Do not worry about neat handwriting. A page full of honest, untidy numbers is far more useful than a beautiful empty book.

Record-keeping is also not the same as accounting. Accountants prepare formal statements for big companies. What you need is simpler: a clear daily list of money in, money out, goods in and goods out. That simple list is enough to answer the big questions: Am I making profit? Which goods should I buy more of? Who owes me? Can I afford this loan?

How they connect

These records are not separate worlds. When you sell a bag of rice for cash, it goes in your **sales record**, your **stock** goes down by one bag, and your **cash book** goes up. When you sell the same bag on credit, sales and stock still change, but instead of the cash book you write it in your **debtors list**. When the customer pays later, the debtors list goes down and the cash book goes up. When you pay a bus driver to carry goods, that is an **expense** and the cash book goes down.
Worked example: Ngozi's provisions shop, three transactions
For example, Ngozi runs a small provisions shop in Enugu. Prices are approximate.
Morning: she sells 2 tins of milk at about ₦1,200 each for cash. Sales record: +₦2,400. Stock of milk: down 2 tins. Cash book: +₦2,400.

Afternoon: Mama Chidi takes a carton of noodles worth about ₦9,500 and promises to pay on Friday. Sales record: +₦9,500. Stock of noodles: down 1 carton. Debtors list: Mama Chidi owes ₦9,500, due Friday.
Evening: Ngozi pays ₦1,500 for a keke to bring new goods. Expenses record: transport ₦1,500. Cash book: minus ₦1,500.
End of day: sales total ₦11,900. Cash book movement: +₦2,400 minus ₦1,500 = +₦900. Debtors: ₦9,500 owed.
Ngozi sold ₦11,900 of goods but only ₦900 more cash is in her hand. Her records explain exactly why, so she will not panic or accuse anyone.
Which records to start with

If five records feel like too much, start with two: the **sales record** and the **expenses record**. These alone let you work out a rough profit. Add the **debtors list** the very first time someone buys on credit, because credit is where traders lose the most money. Add the **stock record** when you have more than a few products. Add the **cash book** when you are ready to check your cash every day.
Keep receipts too

A record is not only what you write. Supplier receipts, POS slips, bank alerts and transfer screenshots are also records. Keep paper receipts in an envelope for each month and write the month on the front. On your phone, make a photo album called "Shop receipts".

Identify one leak in your own business

Traders rarely lose money in one big disaster. Most money leaks out quietly, ₦200 here, ₦1,000 there, a forgotten debt, a helper who "borrows" from the drawer. Each leak looks small. Over a year they can be the difference between a growing shop and one that cannot restock.

Five common leaks
**Forgotten credit.** A customer takes goods and you forget, or you remember a smaller amount than she really owes.
**Eating the capital.** You spend sales money on the house, not knowing part of it was money to restock.
**Selling below cost.** Your supplier raised the price and you did not notice, so you now sell at a loss.
**Missing stock.** Goods are stolen, spoiled or taken by family, and nobody knows how many.
**Untracked small expenses.** Transport, levies, phone data, nylon bags, change for customers. Each is small, together they are large.

Worked example: how much a daily leak really costs
For example, Amina sells drinks and snacks at a motor park and does not record small giveaways and unpaid snacks. Amounts are approximate.
She guesses she loses about ₦500 a day to snacks given on credit that are never paid, and things taken by children.
She works 6 days a week: ₦500 × 6 = ₦3,000 a week.
There are about 52 weeks in a year: ₦3,000 × 52 = ₦156,000.
One crate of soft drinks costs her about ₦6,000, so ₦156,000 is about 26 crates of stock.
A leak she thinks is "nothing" costs her about ₦156,000 a year, enough to buy around 26 crates. Writing it down is the first step to stopping it.
When the supplier raises the price

Prices of goods in Nigerian markets can change quickly. If you buy a bag of sugar for one price this month and a higher price next month, but keep selling at your old price, your profit shrinks or disappears. Without a record of what you paid, you may not notice for weeks. With a record, you see the new cost the same day and can adjust your selling price or buy elsewhere.
Records protect relationships

Arguments over money damage businesses and families. A customer says she paid; you say she did not. Your husband thinks the shop makes plenty; you know it does not. A helper is accused of stealing when the real problem is spoiled goods. A written, dated record settles these arguments calmly. You can show the page instead of raising your voice. When a customer sees you write her credit in front of her and read it back, she is also less likely to dispute it later.
Watch for scams on transfers

Some people show a fake transfer screen or a fake SMS alert and walk away with goods. Before you release goods, check that the money has entered your own account in your bank or wallet app (for example Opay, Moniepoint or your bank app), not just the customer's phone. Record the transfer only after you confirm it.
What records cannot do

Records do not make money by themselves. They show you the truth, and the truth is sometimes uncomfortable: a product you love may be losing money, or a relative may be taking more than you thought. The value comes from acting on what you see. In Module 4 you will learn how to read your records and turn them into decisions.
Stock that walks away

Goods leave a shop in many ways besides sales. Tomatoes spoil in the heat. A child takes a biscuit. A relative collects a bag of rice "for the house". A helper gives a friend a discount you did not agree. None of this is a problem if it is written: you can decide what is fair and what must stop. It becomes a problem only when nobody knows. A simple stock count at the end of each week, compared with what your sales record says you sold, shows you how much stock disappeared without a sale.

Also remember that goods you take for your own family are a real cost to the business. If you take a carton of noodles home, write it down as "taken for home" at what you paid for it. That way your profit figure stays honest, and you can see how much the household is really drawing from the shop each month.

Option 1: the ruled notebook

This is the classic method. You rule columns with a ruler and write each transaction on one line. It suits anyone who can read and write numbers. Use a pen, not a pencil, so entries cannot be rubbed out. If you make a mistake, draw one line through it and write the correct figure next to it; do not tear out pages.
Option 2: the picture and tally book

If reading is hard for you, draw a small picture for each product at the top of a column: a loaf of bread, a bottle of oil, a sachet of water. Each time you sell one, make a tally mark (four lines and a fifth across). Use a coloured pen for credit sales, for example red. At night, count the tallies and multiply by the price, or ask someone you trust to do it with you.
Worked example: Kemi's picture tally for bread
For example, Kemi sells bread and cannot write easily. She sells small loaves at about ₦700 and big loaves at about ₦1,500. Prices are approximate.
She draws a small loaf on the left of the page and a big loaf on the right.
Each sale gets one tally mark under the right picture. Credit sales are marked in red.
At night she counts: small loaf 23 marks (3 in red), big loaf 11 marks (1 in red).
Credit (red): 3 × ₦700 + 1 × ₦1,500 = ₦2,100 + ₦1,500 = ₦3,600, so cash she should have from sales is ₦32,600 minus ₦3,600 = ₦29,000.
With only pictures and marks, Kemi knows she sold about ₦32,600 of bread, should have about ₦29,000 cash, and is owed ₦3,600.
Option 3: the phone

A smartphone can hold your records in a free spreadsheet such as **Google Sheets**, or in a bookkeeping app downloaded from the Google Play Store or App Store. A spreadsheet adds totals for you and saves a copy online if you sign in with a Google account. Before choosing any app, check that it is free or affordable, works offline, lets you export or back up your data, and has good recent reviews. In Module 4 you will set one up step by step.
Protect your phone records

If you keep records on a phone, set a screen lock (PIN or fingerprint). Never share your bank PIN or one-time codes with anyone, including people who say they are from a bank or app. Back up regularly so a lost phone does not mean lost records.
Make it a habit
Choose one fixed time each day to finish your records, for example after closing and before going home.
Keep the notebook and pen in the same place every day.
Write small things immediately; do the adding up at your fixed time.
Once a week, on the same day, add up the whole week.
Show your records to someone you trust once a month so you stay accountable.
Mixing methods sensibly

Many traders get the best of both. During a busy market day, phones are awkward: your hands are full, the screen is hard to see in the sun, and you worry about theft. So write quickly in a small notebook or on a tally sheet, then type the day's totals into your phone in the evening. The notebook is your **original record**; the phone is your **summary and backup**. Keep the notebooks for at least a year, because lenders or partners may want to see them.

Whatever you choose, keep the same layout every day. If your columns move around, totals become confusing and mistakes hide. Copy the column headings onto every new page, or in a phone, keep using the same sheet with the same headings.

Checking at closing time
Add the Total column for the whole day.
Add the cash sales only. Count your cash. Subtract the float (the change money you started with). The difference should equal cash sales.
Open your bank or wallet app. Add today's incoming transfers. They should equal transfer sales.
Check that every credit sale also appears in your debtors list.
If something does not match, write the difference and a short note (for example "₦500 short, maybe wrong change").
Use your bank alerts

Your bank or wallet app keeps a history of every transfer you receive. At closing, scroll through today's credits and tick each one against a transfer line in your sales book. Unmatched alerts often mean you forgot to write a sale.

Do not expect a perfect match every day. Small differences happen from wrong change or a sale you forgot. What matters is that you notice them. If you are short by a few hundred naira once a month, that is normal. If you are short almost every day, something is wrong: a pricing mistake, a helper's error, or theft. Your sales book is how you find out.
Returns and discounts

Sometimes a customer brings goods back, or you give a discount to close a sale. Write these honestly. For a return, write a new line with the item and the amount in brackets, for example (2,800), and take it away from the day's total. For a discount, write the price you actually received, not the shelf price. If you write the shelf price, your sales book will say you earned more than you did, and your cash will never match.

If a helper sells for you, ask her to use the same book and the same columns. At closing, go through the lines together. This is not about suspicion; it is how both of you can prove the shop's money is correct.

At the end of each page, write the page total at the bottom and carry it to the top of the next page as "brought forward". This way, the last page of the day shows the full day's total without you adding every page again.

The formula in words

**Opening stock + stock bought − stock sold = stock that should be left.** Count what is actually left. If it is less, the difference is a loss. Your stock card also tells you when to buy. Look at how much you sell in a normal week. Knowing this figure matters when you calculate profit in Module 4 and when a lender asks how big your business is.

If your helper sells while you are away, a stock count before you leave and after you return is the fairest check for both of you. Write both counts on the card and sign them together. Disagreements become rare when the numbers are agreed on the spot.

You do not need a stock card for every tiny item. Start with your five most expensive or fastest moving products, since these carry the most money. Small items can be counted as a group, for example "sweets jar" or "seasoning cubes box".

Age your debts

Set credit rules
**Who**: only regular customers you know well, with a working phone number.
**How much**: a limit per person, for example no more than one week's typical purchase.
**How long**: a clear payment date, usually within a week or two.
**One at a time**: no new credit until the last debt is paid, or at least reduced.
**Write it every time**: no credit sale without a line in the list.

On the due date, send a short WhatsApp or SMS: "Good morning Ma, this is Chioma from the fabric shop. A reminder that the balance of ₦8,000 is due today. Thank you for your custom." Being polite, specific and on time works better than waiting until you are angry.

If your supplier gives you goods and you pay later, keep a separate page called **creditors** (people you owe), with the same columns: date, supplier, goods, amount, due date, paid, balance. Paying suppliers on time builds your reputation, and a supplier who trusts you may offer better prices or larger credit. Before you accept supplier credit, check from your sales summary that you will sell enough in time to pay.

If you buy something that lasts a long time for the business, such as a table, a freezer, a weighing scale or a sewing machine, write it on a separate **equipment** page with date and price. It is a business cost, but because it lasts for years, do not count the full price against one week's profit. Simply keep the record so you know what the business owns and what it cost.

Some costs come once a month or once a year: shop rent, association dues, a generator service, a trade fair stand. These are easy to forget when you look at one week, and then they arrive as a shock. Write a short list at the front of your expenses section of every cost that comes monthly or yearly, with the usual amount and the month it is due. Each week, set aside a small part toward them. For example, if stall rent is about ₦60,000 a year, putting aside about ₦1,200 a week (₦60,000 ÷ 52, rounded) means the rent is ready when it is due.

Watch prices too. When you record a stock purchase, write the quantity and the unit price, not only the total. Next time you buy, compare. If the price of a bag has gone up, you will see it the same day and can adjust your selling price before your profit disappears.

Profit per item: markup and margin

For each main product you need two numbers: what you **pay** for it (cost price) and what you **sell** it for (selling price). The difference is your **gross profit per item**. Traders talk about this in two ways. **Markup** compares profit with the cost price. **Margin** compares profit with the selling price. They are easy to mix up, so use one consistently.
Worked example: Ifeoma's two products
For example, Ifeoma sells household goods in Onitsha. Prices are approximate.
Detergent pack: costs ₦1,500, sells for ₦1,800. Profit per pack: ₦300. Markup: ₦300 ÷ ₦1,500 = 0.20, so 20%. Margin: ₦300 ÷ ₦1,800 = about 0.17, so about 17%.
Plastic bowl set: costs ₦4,000, sells for ₦6,000. Profit per set: ₦2,000. Markup: ₦2,000 ÷ ₦4,000 = 50%. Margin: ₦2,000 ÷ ₦6,000 = about 33%.
From her product count, she sells about 60 detergent packs a week and 5 bowl sets.
Weekly profit from detergent: 60 × ₦300 = ₦18,000. From bowls: 5 × ₦2,000 = ₦10,000.
The bowls have the higher margin, but detergent brings more total profit because it sells fast. Ifeoma keeps detergent always in stock and displays the bowls better to sell more of them.
Warning signs to watch
Sales falling for two or more months in a row without a clear reason.
Cash shortages appearing most days, not just occasionally.
Stock gaps growing every week.
Debts older than four weeks increasing.
Your weekly drawing larger than your weekly profit.
Supplier prices rising while your selling prices stay the same.
One finding, one action

Do not try to fix everything at once. Each month, choose the single most important finding and decide one clear action with a date, for example: "From Monday, no new credit to anyone owing more than two weeks." Write it at the top of next month's page and check it at month end.
Comparing over time

A single month tells you little. Patterns appear when you compare: this month with last month, this December with last December, this week with the same week last month. Many traders notice that sales follow the calendar: school resumption, salary week at month end, festive seasons, rainy season. Once you see your own pattern in your own records, you can buy stock before the busy period and keep costs low in the slow period.

Also compare your records with your feelings. Many traders feel that a product is their best seller because customers ask about it often. The records may show something else. Trust the numbers, but use your experience to explain them. The best decisions come from both together.
Turning a finding into a price decision

Records also help you set prices. When a supplier raises the cost of an item, check your margin. If detergent rises from ₦1,500 to ₦1,650 and you still sell at ₦1,800, your profit per pack falls from ₦300 to ₦150, half of what it was. At 60 packs a week, that is ₦9,000 less profit every week. You might raise your price a little, look for another supplier, or accept a smaller margin on purpose to keep customers. The record does not decide for you, but it shows you exactly what each choice costs.

Look at your running costs as a share of sales too. If transport is ₦9,000 out of ₦150,000 weekly sales, that is about 6 naira in every 100. If it rises to 10 naira in every 100, it is time to look for a cheaper way to move goods.
Finally, share what you learn with someone you trust: a fellow trader, a cooperative leader, a WODDI mentor. Explaining your numbers out loud often helps you see what to do next.

**Profit** is what the business earns after paying for the goods it sold and all its running costs. A **loss** is when costs are bigger than sales. To calculate it properly for a month, you need four records: your sales total, your stock purchases, your stock count at the start and end of the month, and your running costs.

Profit is what remains after the cost of goods sold and running costs.
Why stock counts matter

If you buy ₦400,000 of goods this month but sell only part of them, it is wrong to count the whole ₦400,000 against this month's sales. The unsold goods are still on your shelf and still have value. So you calculate the **cost of goods sold**, the cost of only what actually left the shop.

Each step removes one kind of cost until only true profit remains.
The three formulas
**Cost of goods sold** = opening stock (at cost) + stock purchases − closing stock (at cost).
**Gross profit** = sales − cost of goods sold.
**Net profit** = gross profit − running costs (transport, rent, levies, packaging, phone, staff, charges, bad debts).

Value stock at what you **paid**, not at your selling price. Count sales as all goods sold this month, including credit sales. If a debt becomes clearly unrecoverable, count it as a running cost called **bad debt**. Your drawings are **not** a running cost; they come out of net profit afterwards.
Worked example: Halima's October profit
For example, Halima's provisions stall. All amounts are approximate.
Sales for October (cash, transfer and credit): ₦744,000.
Opening stock on 1 October, counted and valued at cost: ₦150,000.
Stock purchases in October: ₦520,000.
Closing stock on 31 October, at cost: ₦170,000.
Running costs: transport ₦36,000 + levy ₦7,200 + packaging ₦9,600 + phone ₦6,000 + helper ₦12,000 + bank and POS charges ₦3,200 + one bad debt ₦4,000 = ₦78,000.
Halima's net profit for October is about ₦166,000. She drew ₦80,000 during the month, so about ₦86,000 stayed in the business as extra capital.
Profit versus cash

Your profit and the change in your cash will rarely be the same. In Halima's month, stock on the shelf grew by ₦20,000 (from ₦150,000 to ₦170,000), which used cash but is not a cost. Customers may owe more at the end than at the start, which counts as sales but is not yet cash. This is why a trader can be profitable and still short of cash, or have plenty of cash while making a loss. You need both the profit calculation and the cash book.

Can you afford the repayment?

Before you borrow, use your own records to check that the business can repay from **profit**, not from capital. A loan used to buy stock should increase sales and profit by more than the repayment, otherwise it makes you poorer.
Worked example: should Esther take this loan?
For example, Esther's drinks business is offered a loan with a monthly repayment. Amounts are approximate.
Her records show average monthly net profit of about ₦120,000.
Her monthly drawing for the household is ₦80,000.
Profit left after drawing: ₦120,000 − ₦80,000 = ₦40,000 a month.
The loan repayment would be ₦55,000 a month.
₦55,000 is more than ₦40,000, so she is short by ₦15,000 every month unless the loan raises her profit by at least that much.
Esther asks for a smaller loan or a longer period, or plans exactly how the extra stock will raise profit by more than ₦15,000 a month, before she signs anything.
Avoid loan scams

Never pay a "processing fee" to someone who calls or messages you offering a loan or grant. Never share your BVN, card PIN or one-time codes with anyone. Before using a loan app, check that it appears on the list of approved digital lenders published by the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC). Read the total amount you will repay, not only the monthly figure.
Grants and programmes

Grant and support programmes for small businesses and women entrepreneurs appear from time to time, run by government, development agencies, banks and non-profits. Application forms often ask for monthly sales, number of customers or how you will use the money. Answer only with figures from your records, and keep a copy of what you submitted. Be wary of any "grant" that asks you to pay first.
Telling your business story with numbers

When you speak to a lender or a programme, use your records to tell a short, clear story: what you sell, for how long, your average monthly sales, your typical monthly profit, and exactly how the money would be used and how it would increase profit. For example: "I sell provisions in the same market. My average sales over six months are about ₦700,000 a month and net profit about ₦150,000. With ₦300,000 more stock before December I expect higher festive sales, based on last December's records." Figures from your own books are far more convincing than promises.
Partners and suppliers

A supplier deciding whether to give you goods on credit, or a person considering joining your business, will trust records they can see. Show them your monthly summaries and your history of paying suppliers on time from your creditors page. If you go into partnership, agree in writing how profit will be shared and how records will be kept, and give each partner access to the books.

There are also free and paid bookkeeping apps made for small businesses, including some built for Nigerian traders. Apps come and go, so instead of trusting a name, check these points before you put your business records in one:

Does it work offline when your data is finished or the network is poor?
Can you export or download your records (for example as a spreadsheet or PDF)?

Does it ask for permissions it does not need, such as your contacts or photos, for no clear reason?

Lock your phone with a PIN or fingerprint. Never share your Google password or one-time codes. Do not keep bank PINs or passwords in your spreadsheet. If several people need access, share the sheet only with people you trust, and you can give them view-only access.

Google Sheets keeps your file in your Google account, so if your phone is lost you can sign in on a new phone and find it. For apps, check whether backup is automatic or something you must switch on.
